title: Upset Magnitude Analysis
text:
Figure 1





This visualization examines the magnitude of true upsets in ATP matches, defined as the rank gap between the winner and loser (winner rank – loser rank), segmented by the winner’s ranking cohort: Top 50, Ranks 51–100, and 101+. The distribution shows how “big” upsets tend to be depending on who is pulling them off. The width of each violin reflects how varied the upset sizes are, while the embedded line and dot represent the median and interquartile range.
A clear pattern emerges: Top 50 winners tend to produce the smallest upset magnitudes, both in median size and overall spread. This indicates that when elite players secure upsets over higher-ranked opponents, they are usually not overcoming massive ranking deficits, these upsets tend to be modest and tightly clustered. In contrast, players ranked 51–100 and 101+ generate upsets with much larger gaps and more variability, suggesting that when lower-ranked players win, they are more likely to defeat opponents significantly above them in the rankings.
Taken together, the results suggest that upsets are not created equal: elite players rarely generate dramatic upsets because their ranking already reflects consistent performance, while lower-ranked players account for a broader and more dramatic range of ranking reversals. This aligns with the intuitive view that ATP competition is top-heavy, meaning players outside the Top 100 occasionally create striking results, whereas Top 50 athletes tend to compete within a more predictable performance band when upsetting someone above them.

title: Court Surfaces
text:
ATP tournaments are played on three main different surfaces: hard court, clay (green and red), and grass. Specific players often perform better on certain surfaces, because of their game style, the way they grew up, and the types of conditions that they are accustomed to. Most players grow up playing on hard courts, as these are the most plentiful around the world. Certain countries, like Spain, train their players on red clay from the start, which is a surface in which the ball bounces higher and rewards topspin. Finally, grass courts are the rarest surface, yet they carry a rich tradition and tournaments on this surface are considered extremely prestigious. This surface rewards an aggressive playing style, with slices, dropshots, and netplay often utilized.
We are familiar with certain player narratives, such as Nadal dominating on the clay and Federer being the king of grass, and we wanted to see if the data confirmed this.
This first visualization shows the number of titles each player has won on each surface. In comparison to the other players, it is clear that Nadal has won the majority of clay court tournaments. Being from Spain, Nadal has grown up on this surface and has developed a game style that maximizes its advantages. He thrives on long rallies, a high bouncing topsin forehand, and superior movement. His nickname, the “King of Clay,” is strongly supported by the data. Additionally, it is shown that Federer has won the most grass court tournaments out of everyone. Federer has traditionally been a serve-and-volleyer, coming to the net and finishing points quickly. This, along with his deadly slice backhand, has made him especially effective on this surface.









The next visualization investigates the percentage of singles matches won on each surface. It is interesting to note that the data confirms aforementioned narratives such as the notion that Nadal plays much better on clay. Nadal and Sinner have clear surfaces they win more on. It is also interesting to note that some players perform relatively poorly on specific surfaces compared to others, with some examples being Alcaraz clearly performing worse on hard surfaces and Federer playing worse on clay. This visualization effectively shows each player’s objectively best and worst, as well as likely their favorite and least favorite, surfaces to play on.

title: ATP Singles Ranking
text:
The ATP singles ranking is a point-based system that ranks men’s professional tennis players based on their performance in official singles tournaments over a span of 52 weeks. A player’s best 19 tournament results determines their ranking, with points awarded based on the level of the tournament (e.g., Grand Slam, ATP Masters 1000, ATP 500, ATP 250, etc.) and how far a player advances in the tournament. Points from tournaments are dropped after 52 weeks and replaced with current performances, meaning rankings can change weekly. Rankings are important for tournament eligibility and their seeding within the draw. The player with the highest number of points at the end of the year is crowned the year-end No.1 player.
The Big 3, Novak Djokovic, Rafael Nadal, and Roger Federer, have dominated the ATP Tour for the past two decades, a testament to their consistent presence at the top of the singles rankings. The visualization below illustrates the career trajectory for these players’ singles rankings, with circles denoting their Grand Slam victories at each point in time. Federer dominated the early years, particularly from 2005-2010, as shown by a cluster of green circles coinciding with his peak ranking. On the other hand, Nadal’s Grand Slam wins appear to be more evenly distributed across his career, without any distinct ‘domination’ period. Djokovic, meanwhile, seems to find his prime later than both Federer and Nadal, reflecting his later rise to the top and younger age compared to the other two.









The New 2, Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner, have risen to the top of the game in the last few years, bringing new faces to the men’s tennis landscape. Both have established themselves as standouts of the younger generation, challenging the dominance of older players. The visualization below shows the ATP singles ranking trajectory for Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner, with circles representing their Grand Slam wins. Alcaraz emerged as a front runner, rising to the top of the game slightly before Sinner, accumulating a few more Grand Slam titles during this time period. However, Sinner has recently surged ahead in the rankings, signaling the beginning of a fierce rivalry for the world No. 1 spot between these two rising stars.









Beyond visualizing the movement of these five players’ singles rankings over time, we can also examine the percentage of weeks each player has spent at the No. 1 spot throughout their career. The bar chart below highlights such data, showcasing how Djokovic has spent approximately 37.1% of his career as the world No. 1. This is evidence of his sustained dominance at the top of the game and consistency year after year, as rankings are a great data-driven measure of performance based on a player’s results against a variety of different opponents.
It is also interesting to note how Djokovic, Federer, and Nadal make up around 80% of the total weeks spent at No. 1 in their careers. This remarkable statistic not only underscores their individual dominance, but their role in defining modern men’s tennis.

title: Page example
section: Header Level 2: Tips for linking/displaying figures and images.
text:
Header Level 2: Tips for linking/displaying figures and images.

Header Level 3: Linking to a Plot/Fig

Write you code to create your plot and save it. Save this script in src/figs. The source code does not need to be on the website.
Ensure that your plot is saved to figs/ by referencing the path with {here}.
At the top of the .qmd file for your page, add a code block that source()s the script that will generate the plot you wish displayed on that page.

For example:
source(here::here("figs", "point_mpg_by_wt.R"))`
Make sure to edit the code block so that the code runs only (no output).
NOTE: Code blocks that appear in .qmd files will call .R files only. Do NOT embed code blocks in your .qmd file(s) that will process data or create plots directly. Reserve .qmd files for website text, sourcing script files, and calling .png plot files. Developers and engineers compartmentalize project elements and do not combine all content into a single files. Doing so creates many problems not limited to code breaking and code-repair problems, Git merge problems, etc. You will follow a similar practice of breaking the project into pieces, save those files, and push them to the remote repository weekly for your team members.
This code-source()ing step also ensures that plot(s) are (re)created when Quarto rendering the website build files. You certainly want this feature so that new website elements and files are built during the rendering process. A full website re-build, however, is unnecessary when no element of the website changes other than the images and figures embedded within it. As a result, re-builds are not always necessary and will increase update time.

title: Page example
section: Header Level 2: (Optional) Circumventing a Full Website Build
text:
Header Level 2: (Optional) Circumventing a Full Website Build
Sometimes the main structure of your website is untouched but you have new data and you need to run a rebuild of your plots. Although re-rendering is not problematic, it might just take longer than you desire. If you don’t need to render the website and just want to build files, the following is a solution, though requires some extra work.
To avoid a full site rebuild (re-render) when you simply want to create and git push new plots:

Add your source()ing code to a separate file, for example, call_scripts/call_plot_scripts.qmd.
Add a code block to source individual .R files or all .R files in a directory.

Example:
#| include: false

# source a script file that this page depends on
source(here::here("figs", "point_mpg_by_wt.R"))

This .qmd file will render and create the .png files you need in your specified directory but the page will not be linked on your website. Technically, it will be visible at https://the_url/call_scripts/call_plot_scripts.html but this will be difficult to find. You can always remove the file or directory after rendering the website if you want to remove it completely.


Link the plot .png file in your .qmd file.

Once you know the name and location of the file, you can reference it like this, where the .png file is being pulled from figs/:



a plot description

title: Country Dominance
text:
The visualization below explores the historical match-win totals for five leading tennis nations, the United States, Spain, France, Italy, and Germany, spanning from 1968 to 2025. This broader international perspective highlights how different eras of tennis greatness have been shaped by the strength of national player cohorts. The United States stands out most prominently in the earlier decades, showing a dramatic peak in match wins throughout the 1970s and 1980s. This reflects a golden generation of American tennis led by icons such as Jimmy Connors, John McEnroe, and later Pete Sampras and Andre Agassi.
As we move toward the 2000s, a noticeable shift occurs in the competitive landscape. Match-win totals across countries become more balanced, signaling globalization of the sport and the rise of strong tennis cultures beyond the United States. Spain emerges as a new powerhouse, driven by clay-court depth and the sustained success of Rafael Nadal and other top Spanish players. France, Italy, and Germany all remain steady contenders, collectively contributing to an increasingly competitive field where success is distributed more evenly across nations.
This graph not only demonstrates the changing dominance in men’s tennis over time but also reflects how the rise of new generations and training infrastructures around the world continues to reshape the sport’s competitive dynamics.









As the era of the “Big 3” comes to a close, the rise of young stars like Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner signals a new chapter in men’s tennis. With their rapid climb to the top of the rankings and early Grand Slam success, they appear poised to reshape the competitive landscape, continuing the trend of a more globally distributed field. Instead of a single dominant nation or trio of players, the future of tennis may be defined by tighter rivalries, more frequent shifts at the top, and increased representation from emerging tennis countries. This transition suggests a sport entering a more unpredictable and thrilling era, one where the next generation has the opportunity to redefine what sustained excellence looks like on the global stage.

title: ATP Doubles
text:
In tennis, doubles involves two teams of two players competing on one court. Unlike singles, where players compete alone, doubles requires teamwork, communication, and a slightly different set of skills. The court is wider in doubles, with both alleys in play, allowing for different angles and more space to attack and defend. Doubles players often have great volleys, quick reflexes, and a wider range of different shots in their repertoire. Being able to react quickly during fast exchanges is a big part of what makes doubles so exciting to watch. Playing doubles often enhances a player’s net game in singles, which is why so many of the top singles players continue to compete in doubles tournaments.
The visualization below shows the number of doubles titles each of our featured players has won over the course of their career. In comparison to their impressive singles achievements, the number of doubles titles they’ve earned are minimal. Rafael Nadal has the most doubles titles to his name, with 11 over the course of his career. Roger Federer is not far behind with 8 doubles titles, and Novak Djokovic only has 1. Although both Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner are at the early stages in their career, they both have zero doubles titles. The average number of doubles titles among these five players are 4.









The graph below shows that these players have not dominated the doubles tour as much as they have in the singles tour. As the caption mentions, the solid colors represent the percentage of doubles matches won, while the faded colors represent matches lost. Federer and Nadal barely have a wining record, whereas Djokovic and Sinner have a losing record. Alcaraz has not played any doubles matches at this point in his career. The ATP tour has doubles specialists, which are players that only focus on training and playing doubles. Our featured players focus on playing singles, which is why their winning record in doubles is not as impressive.









Although these players have played a few doubles tournaments in their career, it is important to take a look at the timing of these matches. The visualization below shows the total number of doubles matches the Big 3 have played per year. Sinner and Alcaraz have not played enough doubles matches to be included in this visualization. Federer played the most out of everyone at the start of his career, with around 40 total doubles matches in the year 2000. This number just gradually decreased as his career progressed. The dotted lines represent the year each player won their first singles grand slam. It is interesting to note how the number of doubles matches they each played began to decrease after their singles career took off. The Big 3’s shift away from doubles reflects a common pattern among top singles players, as their career goals become focused on overall singles dominance.









Finally, the visualization below puts into perspective the number of matches each player has played in singles (solid colors) vs doubles (faded colors). It is clear that the majority of their career has been spent playing singles tournaments. While doubles tennis has its own set of champions, the spotlight in the sport is overwhelmingly focused on the singles players, especially these five.

title: Performance Over Time
text:
A tennis player’s career often follows a rise-peak-decline pattern. One’s early career is generally focused on improving skills, gaining experience, and learning how to compete at the top of the game. Tournament wins are often sporadic during the beginning years of their career. During the middle stage of players careers, they tend to perform their best and accumulate the most Grand Slam wins and career highlights. Late in a career, the player’s physical abilities often decline, leading to longer recovery times and increased injury risk. At this point in time, it is important for players to adapt their game style and focus on playing fewer events. Historically, women have peaked earlier in their careers (around ages 22–26), whereas men tend to peak later. Factors that can affect one’s performance over time include physical condition and injuries, playing style, mental toughness, and experience.
The visualization below is a heatmap showing the number of singles matches each selected player has played each year. The darker tiles indicate more matches played, whereas the lighter tiles indicate less matches played that year. As shown by the Big 3, the highest match volume occurred early in their careers, roughly 5 years in. The lowest match volume appears at both the beginning and end of each player’s career, which makes sense. We expect to see a similar pattern for the New 2 as their careers evolve. Playing more matches can indicate a player’s growing confidence, greater success, and/or participation in a larger number of tournaments. However, this places significant mental and physical demands that often affect performance in later years.









This next visualization is a facet plot highlighting each player’s performance by age. Performance is measured as the percentage of singles matches won. Both Federer and Djokovic appear to reach their peak performance — winning roughly 80% of matches — around the age of 25. Nadal’s peak occurs slightly earlier, around age 22, with a somewhat lower maximum win percentage. It is interesting to note how these three curves follow the same rise-peak-decline pattern that was introduced earlier. Because Sinner and Alcaraz are newer to the tour and much younger, their performance patterns are different from the Big 3. Sinner appears to currently be in the “peak” stage of his career, with his winning percentage increasing every year. Alcaraz shows a slight downward slope in the current data, but is expected to continue improving, as he is still early in his career.









Below is a timeline showing the end-of-career milestones for the Big 3. There are three key markers: the last Grand Slam won, the last title won that was not a Grand Slam, and the last match played (retirement). Federer’s timeline shows an approximately equal spacing between these events, with about two years between each milestone. This indicates a gradual winding down, rather than a sudden drop in performance. Nadal, on the other hand, won a Grand Slam as his final tournament before retirement. This indicates how some players like to retire on a high note. Both players retired roughly three years after their last Grand Slam victory. Djokovic is the only member of the Big 3 still active on the tour, which is why he does not have a “retirement” marker. While he has not won a Grand Slam since the US Open in 2023, his continued presence on the tour demonstrates competitiveness at the highest level. However, will he follow the same pattern of retiring approximately three years after the last Grand Slam title? Or will he be able to break the trend and continue to sustain elite performance? Only time will tell.

title: Team Tennis
text:
Professional tennis has given us legends, created fierce rivalries, and given us unforgettable matches. This site uses data visualizations to bring such stories to life, and to highlight patterns, rivalries, and the evolution of the sport.
At the center of modern tennis history stands Roger Federer, Rafael Nadal, and Novak Djokovic, also known as the Big Three. Their rivalry has defined an era, producing countless wins, each pushing each each other to new heights. Together, they’ve amassed dozens of Grand Slam titles, spent record-breaking weeks at World No. 1, and redefined what dominance looks like in tennis.
Now that two of the Big Three players have retired, a new rivalry has began to take stage. Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner are not just rising stars, they’re the future of the sport. With data-driven insights, we’ll explore how their early careers compare to the Big Three, and what their budding rivalry might mean for the future of tennis.
Our data stretches back over six decades and includes every player since 1963: their names, heights, countries of origin, and every match detail from the ATP tour. By combining rich historical records with modern performance metrics, this project offers both context and clarity to tennis’s biggest debates.

title: Team Tennis
text:
Get to know the players:

Roger Federer Roger Federer is a Swiss tennis player, born in 1981 in Basel. He became one of the sport’s greatest champions with 20 Grand Slam titles, highlighted by a record 8 at Wimbledon. He held the world No. 1 ranking for 310 weeks, earned two Olympic medals, and retired in 2022 after more than two decades at the top of the game.


Rafael Nadal Rafael Nadal is a Spanish tennis legend, born in 1986 in Manacor, Mallorca. He turned pro in 2001, and over his career amassed 22 Grand Slam singles titles, including a record 14 at the French Open. He has 92 ATP singles titles in total, spent 209 weeks as world No. 1, and dominated on the clay courts before retiring in 2024.


Novak Djokovic Novak Djokovic is a Serbian tennis player, born in 1987 in Belgrade. Novak has won a record 24 Grand Slam titles, including 10 Australian Opens. He has held the world No. 1 ranking for a record 428 weeks, and has established himself as one of the most accomplished and dominant players in tennis history.


Carlos Alcaraz Carlos Alcaraz is a Spanish tennis player, born in 2003 in El Palmar, Murcia. Carlos turned professional in 2018, and by the age of 22, has already won six Grand Slam singles titles — French Open (2024, 2025), Wimbledon (2023, 2024), and US Open (2022, 2025). He has risen to the world No. 1 ranking, which was first achieved in 2022 and again in 2025.


Jannik Sinner Jannik Sinner is an Italian tennis player, born in 2001 in San Candido. Jannik turned pro in 2018, and by the age of 24, has already won 4 Grand Slam singles titles — Australian Open (2024, 2025), US Open (2024), and Wimbledon (2025). He reached the world No. 1 ranking in 2024, and has claimed 24 ATP Tour-level singles titles overall, marking him as one of the top rising stars and most accomplished young players in men’s tennis.

title: Final Conclusions
text:
Through this process, we have analyzed many different variables including tournament titles, surface types, singles rankings, doubles success, early in career performance, country dominance, and different conditional probabilities. Our analysis has shown that Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner are on career trajectories that closely mirror or even surpass the performances of the Big 3 (Novak Djokovic, Rafael Nadal, and Roger Federer).









Both Alcaraz and Sinner have demonstrated impressive consistency and results especially in their first few years on the ATP Tour. Their total number of wins in this early stage of their careers are on par with or ahead of the Big 3, signaling that the “New 2” are well on track to make a significant impact in the sport of tennis. Additionally, their recent Grand Slam performances have been remarkable. Sinner and Alcaraz have ruled the big stage, with no other player winning a Grand Slam in recent years. This is the same level of dominance that the Big 3 established early in their career.









While sustained success over a full 20+ year career is needed to establish a lasting legacy, the early career win rates of both Alcaraz and Sinner suggest that tennis fans have much to look forward to as this new generation begins to challenge the Big 3’s long-held dominance.









As the sport evolves, it’s clear that Alcaraz and Sinner have the potential to write the next great chapter in tennis history. Their early successes set the stage for a very exciting future, and we will be watching closely to see how the rest of their careers unfold. However, will another player emerge to join Alcaraz and Sinner in creating a modern version of the “Big 3”? Only time will tell, as the next few years will be pivotal in shaping the future of men’s professional tennis.

title: Home Court Advantage
text:
The visualization below compares American players’ win percentages at the US Open and the Australian Open from 2000 to 2025, offering insight into potential home-court advantage over time, and if it even exists. In the early 2000s, the Americans were playing very strongly at the US open, with win rates hovering above 60% and peaking near 70%. However, that advantage noticeably declined throughout the 2010s, with performance at both tournaments converging around the 40–50% mark as global competition intensified.
Interestingly, the past few years show a resurgence, particularly at the Australian Open, where American win percentages have climbed sharply again. Together, these trends suggest that while home-court advantage remains a factor in Grand Slam performance, there are many other factors that can influence whether a player wins a specific match. Players, no matter the nationality, have learned to adapt to changing environments and have had success winning anywhere in the world.

title: Early Career
text:
This visualization compares how five top ATP players — Roger Federer, Rafael Nadal, Novak Djokovic, Carlos Alcaraz, and Jannik Sinner — accumulated singles match wins over the first seven seasons of their careers. By aligning each player’s debut season as “Career Year 1,” we can directly compare development across eras. Using ATP match results from 1998–2024, the cumulative totals reveal not just year-to-year success but how quickly each player established winning momentum on tour. The line chart clearly highlights differences in career trajectories: Federer’s early seasons show a more gradual rise before his dominance took shape, while Nadal and Djokovic accelerated sharply around Years 4 and 5, matching their early Grand Slam breakthroughs.
What stands out most is how rapidly Alcaraz and Sinner are climbing compared to the Big 3 at the same stage. Their steep lines suggest they are matching — or even surpassing — the pace set by three of the greatest players in tennis history. Of course, there are limitations: Alcaraz and Sinner have incomplete careers ahead and fewer injury setbacks so far, and all wins are treated equally regardless of tournament level. Still, the data strongly indicates a generational shift underway. If their current trajectories continue, today’s young stars may well be on track to define the next era of men’s tennis.









This visualization compares early-career performance by age — specifically match wins from ages 17 to 21 — for five top ATP players: Federer, Nadal, Djokovic, Alcaraz, and Sinner. Unlike the previous graph that aligned careers by season, this approach focuses purely on age to highlight who broke through earliest. Nadal stands out immediately with exceptional teenage success, leading the group at ages 17 and 18 — a reflection of his precocious dominance on clay and quick rise to the top of the sport. Federer’s development is much slower in comparison, but by age 21 his match-win count surges past everyone else, showing how his ascent came slightly later yet still reached a remarkable peak. Djokovic follows a steadier trajectory, climbing consistently from 18 to 19 and maintaining solid success each year without the dramatic early highs of Nadal.
Alcaraz and Sinner, representing the new generation, display rapid progression that places them on a historically impressive pace. Alcaraz’s jump at age 18 and Sinner’s strong rise through age 20 show they are already competing at elite levels comparable to the Big 3 at similar ages. While each player’s curve follows a different path — early dominance (Nadal), late explosion (Federer), steady rise (Djokovic), and fast-tracked success (Alcaraz and Sinner) — the takeaway is that greatness develops in multiple forms. Even with limitations such as differing match opportunities and rounded ages, the strong upward trends for Alcaraz and Sinner suggest that they may be poised to define the next era of men’s tennis.

title: Player Performance in Major vs. Non Major Tournaments
text:
This page continues to focus on the Big 3 (Djokovic, Federer, Nadal) and the New 2 (Alcaraz & Sinner). The plots included here look at each player’s performance at different types of tournaments.
There are four major tournaments (Grand Slams) every calendar year, including the US Open, French Open, Australian Open, and Wimbledon. These are the most coveted and prestigious titles, due to a large pot of prize money, the most ranking points, and the global recognition that comes along with winning them. Besides the Grand Slams, there are non-major tournaments that occur almost every weekend. These include a variety of different leveled tournaments, including Master’s 1000s, 500s, 250s, etc. In the visualization below, we look at how these five players’ winning percentages are distributed between the two categories (major vs. non-major).










For all five players, the difference between their major and non-major winning percentage is pretty thin. There is around a 5% increase in win percentage while playing in major tournaments. While it may be counter intuitive that these players have a higher win percentage in major tournaments, it likely signals that more competitive environments bring out the best from these five dominant athletes.
It also may be a phenomenon with the more talented players, as top ranked competitors have less of an incentive to participate in non-major tournaments. They often do not need to rack up ranking points to get into Grand Slams, and use that time to prioritize training, recovery, and rest. This would likely increase the amount of matches played within major tournaments especially during the prime of their careers.
The next visualization investigates the total number of tournaments that each player has won, split between major and non-majors.










This graph exhibits the number of total singles tournaments won on the y axis, as well as with an annotation on the top of each bar. This graph is more intuitive, with each player racking up more non-major tournament wins than major tournament wins. It is very interesting to note that all players have around a 1:3 or 1:4 major to non-major ratio, except for Jannik Sinner. Djokovic has positioned himself as the player with the most Grand Slam titles, and is the only member of the Big 3 that has yet to retire. This suggests he may continue to win more tournaments if the New 2 do not stand in his way.
Again, an important limitation of looking at total career patterns within this group of players is that the Big 3 have had a long and successful career, while Sinner and Alcaraz are just at the beginning of their careers. However, we can see from these visualizations that the New 2 are already making significant strides at the beginning stages of their careers.

title: Straight Set Win Rates
text:
Figure 1





This bar chart compares the likelihood of winning in straight sets based on the winner’s ranking cohort: Top 10 players versus players ranked outside the Top 50, with performance split by the opponent’s ranking group (Top 50 versus 51+). The results show that both ranking groups perform similarly against players ranked outside the Top 50, with straight-set win rates hovering in the mid-50% range. This suggests that players of all rankings tend to dominate lower-ranked opponents at roughly comparable levels, regardless of whether they are elite or simply above average.
However, a notable divergence appears when the opponent is ranked inside the Top 50. In these more competitive matchups, Top 10 players exhibit a significantly higher straight-set win rate, outperforming their outside-Top-50 counterparts by roughly 15 percentage points. This illustrates a structural separation between skill tiers: elite players not only win more often overall, but when they do win, they do so more decisively, even against high-level competition.
Overall, this analysis reinforces the competitive hierarchy within professional tennis. When facing weaker opponents, decisive victories are common across the board; however, against stronger opponents, elite players display far more consistency and match control, while lower-ranked players are more likely to require long, multi-set battles or lose outright. This distinction highlights how straight-set dominance is a meaningful indicator of both skill level and match pressure management.
